strings.hub.mass.title: The Holy Mass
strings.hub.mass.subtitle: The Church's central act of worship
strings.hub.mass.intro: The same sacrifice offered on Calvary, made present on the altar; the Word proclaimed and the Bread broken. Here is how the Mass is ordered, and the sacred things used within it.
strings.sec.structure.title: The Structure of the Mass
strings.sec.structure.summary: Four movements, from the gathering of the people to the sending out.
strings.stepper.structure.title: The Order of Mass
strings.stepper.structure.intro: The Mass unfolds in a clear order — two great tables, the Word and the Eucharist, framed by the rites that gather and send the assembly.
strings.stepper.structure.intro.title: Introductory Rites
strings.stepper.structure.intro.body: The gathering: the entrance procession, the sign of the cross and greeting, the Penitential Act, the Gloria, and the opening prayer that gathers the assembly before God.
strings.stepper.structure.word.title: Liturgy of the Word
strings.stepper.structure.word.body: God speaks: the readings from Scripture, the Responsorial Psalm, the Gospel, the homily, the Profession of Faith (Creed) and the Prayer of the Faithful.
strings.stepper.structure.eucharist.title: Liturgy of the Eucharist
strings.stepper.structure.eucharist.body: The heart of the Mass: the gifts of bread and wine are prepared and offered, the Eucharistic Prayer consecrates them into the Body and Blood of Christ, and the faithful receive Holy Communion.
strings.stepper.structure.concluding.title: Concluding Rites
strings.stepper.structure.concluding.body: The sending: a final blessing and the dismissal — “Go forth, the Mass is ended” — from the Latin of which (Ite, missa est) the very word “Mass” is drawn.
strings.sec.procession.title: The Entrance Procession
strings.sec.procession.summary: The ministers enter in an order that expresses reverence, unity, and the journey toward the altar.
strings.stepper.procession.title: Who Walks In, and Why
strings.stepper.procession.intro: The Entrance Procession is the opening rite of the Mass. The ministers enter the church in an order that expresses reverence, unity, and the journey toward the altar where Christ is present.
strings.stepper.procession.thurifer.title: Thurible Bearer
strings.stepper.procession.thurifer.body: The thurible bearer leads with burning incense, a sign of our prayers rising up to God.
strings.stepper.procession.cross.title: Cross Bearer
strings.stepper.procession.cross.body: The processional cross leads the ministers forward, the sign of Christ who goes before us.
strings.stepper.procession.candle.title: Candle Bearers
strings.stepper.procession.candle.body: Acolytes carry lit candles beside the cross — Christ, the Light of the World.
strings.stepper.procession.bell.title: Bell Ringer
strings.stepper.procession.bell.body: A bell is rung to announce the procession and to call the faithful to worship.
strings.stepper.procession.book.title: Book Bearer
strings.stepper.procession.book.body: The Book of the Gospels is carried aloft — the Word of God proclaimed in the Mass.
strings.stepper.procession.priest.title: The Priest
strings.stepper.procession.priest.body: The priest follows as the one who presides. He represents Christ himself, the Head of the Church.
strings.sec.mass.monstrance.title: The Monstrance
strings.sec.mass.monstrance.summary: Base, shaft, sunburst and luna — the parts of the vessel of Eucharistic adoration.
strings.art.monstrance.title: The Monstrance
strings.art.monstrance.lead: The vessel that displays the Blessed Sacrament for adoration.
strings.art.monstrance.p1: The monstrance — from the Latin monstrare, “to show” — is a sacred vessel that holds the consecrated Host up for the faithful to see and adore. It is used for Eucharistic Adoration, Benediction and processions.
strings.art.monstrance.callout.title: It is not worshipped
strings.art.monstrance.callout.body: The monstrance itself is not adored — it is a sacred vessel that points us to Jesus, truly present in the Eucharist.
strings.art.monstrance.li_cross: **Cross** — at the very top, the sign of our salvation in Christ.
strings.art.monstrance.li_sunburst: **Sunburst (rays of glory)** — the golden rays that represent the radiance of Christ, the “Sun of Justice.”
strings.art.monstrance.li_window: **Ostensorium (the window)** — the central round opening that displays the Eucharist for adoration.
strings.art.monstrance.li_luna: **Luna** — the crescent-shaped clip that holds the Host in place; its shape recalls the moon, a symbol of Our Lady.
strings.art.monstrance.li_host: **The Host** — the Blessed Sacrament itself: the Body, Blood, Soul and Divinity of Jesus Christ.
strings.art.monstrance.li_node: **Node** — the knop on the stem, often worked with wheat and vine — the Bread of Life and the True Vine.
strings.art.monstrance.li_shaft: **Shaft** — the stem that lifts the Host high, our journey in faith raised toward Christ.
strings.art.monstrance.li_base: **Base** — the broad foot that gives stability and honours the sacred presence it bears.
strings.sec.mass.thurible.title: The Thurible
strings.sec.mass.thurible.summary: Bowl, lid, chains and cross — the parts of the censer, and what its smoke means.
strings.art.thurible.title: The Thurible
strings.art.thurible.lead: The censer in which incense is burned, a sign of prayer rising to God.
strings.art.thurible.p1: The thurible is a sacred vessel used to burn incense. The rising smoke is a sign of our prayers ascending to God — “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you” (Psalm 141:2). It is used at the Entrance, the Gospel, the Preparation of the Gifts, the Eucharistic Prayer and Benediction.
strings.art.thurible.callout.title: Why the smoke
strings.art.thurible.callout.body: The incense stands for our prayers, the rising smoke for those prayers ascending to God, and the sweet fragrance honours God and sanctifies the space.
strings.art.thurible.li_finial: **Finial (cross)** — the cross on top, a reminder that our prayers are offered in the name of Christ.
strings.art.thurible.li_lid: **Lid (cover)** — the perforated cover that lets the smoke rise, symbolising prayers ascending to heaven.
strings.art.thurible.li_charcoal: **Charcoal plate** — holds the burning charcoal on which the incense is placed.
strings.art.thurible.li_bowl: **Censer bowl** — the cup that holds the charcoal and incense, the heart of the thurible.
strings.art.thurible.li_chains: **Chains** — usually three, for faith, hope and love; they balance the thurible as it is swung.
strings.art.thurible.li_ring: **Suspension ring** — the ring at the top from which the chains hang.
strings.art.thurible.li_handle: **Handle** — used by the thurifer to raise the lid and swing the thurible during the liturgy.
strings.sec.vessels.title: Sacred Vessels
strings.sec.vessels.summary: Chalice, paten, ciborium and the other vessels that serve at the altar.
strings.art.vessels.title: The Vessels of the Altar
strings.art.vessels.lead: The sacred vessels that hold and carry the Body and Blood of Christ.
strings.art.vessels.p1: Because they hold the Eucharist, the vessels of the altar are made of precious metal (or lined with it), blessed for sacred use, and handled only with reverence.
strings.art.vessels.li_chalice: **Chalice** — the cup that holds the wine which becomes the Blood of Christ.
strings.art.vessels.li_paten: **Paten** — the small plate that holds the priest's host.
strings.art.vessels.li_ciborium: **Ciborium** — the covered cup that holds the hosts for the Communion of the faithful and reserves them in the tabernacle.
strings.art.vessels.li_cruets: **Cruets** — the small jugs of wine and water brought to the altar at the Preparation of the Gifts.
strings.art.vessels.li_pyx: **Pyx** — the small round case used to carry Communion to the sick.
strings.art.vessels.li_luna: **Luna & monstrance** — the crescent clip and the rayed vessel that display the Host for adoration.
strings.art.vessels.callout.title: The linens
strings.art.vessels.callout.body: White cloths serve alongside the vessels: the corporal on which they stand, the purificator for wiping the chalice, and the pall that covers it.
strings.sec.postures.title: Postures & Responses
strings.sec.postures.summary: When to stand, sit and kneel — and the words the people make their own.
strings.art.postures.title: Praying with the Body
strings.art.postures.lead: At Mass the whole body prays. The common postures and responses bind the assembly into one voice.
strings.art.postures.p1: The faithful stand, sit and kneel together at set moments — a shared language of reverence that expresses one faith in one body.
strings.art.postures.li_stand: **Standing** — for prayer and to honour the Gospel; the posture of the risen and attentive.
strings.art.postures.li_sit: **Sitting** — for the readings before the Gospel and the homily, the posture of listening.
strings.art.postures.li_kneel: **Kneeling** — during the Eucharistic Prayer and before Communion, the posture of adoration and humility.
strings.art.postures.li_genuflect: **Genuflection** — bending the right knee toward the tabernacle, adoring Christ present in the Eucharist.
strings.art.postures.li_bow: **Bowing** — a bow of the head at the holy names, and a deeper bow before receiving Communion.
strings.art.postures.li_sign: **The Sign of the Cross** — made at the beginning and end, marking the whole prayer as Christ's.
strings.art.postures.p2: Throughout the Mass the people answer the priest. To “The Lord be with you” they reply “And with your spirit”; the readings close with “Thanks be to God” and “Praise to you, Lord Jesus Christ”; and to the great prayers the assembly seals its assent with “Amen.”
strings.sec.altar.title: The Altar
strings.sec.altar.summary: The table of sacrifice — how it is dressed, the cloths that cover it, and the crosses cut into its stone.
strings.art.altar.title: The Altar
strings.art.altar.lead: At once the table of the Lord's Supper and the altar of his sacrifice — the focus of the whole church.
strings.art.altar.p1: The altar is the heart of the church building. It is at once the table of the Lord's Supper, where the faithful are fed, and the altar of sacrifice, where the offering of Calvary is made present. Because of this the altar stands for Christ himself, and the priest reverences it with a bow and a kiss at the beginning and end of Mass.
strings.art.altar.p2: Nothing is placed on the altar but what the celebration requires. It is dressed simply and with dignity, its ornament following the liturgical colour of the season.
strings.art.altar.li_cross: **The cross** — a cross bearing the figure of the crucified Christ stands on or near the altar, kept in view of the assembly.
strings.art.altar.li_candles: **Candles** — at least two lit candles (up to six, or seven for a bishop) stand on or beside the altar, a sign of reverence and festivity.
strings.art.altar.li_cloth: **The altar cloth** — at least one white cloth covers the altar top, out of reverence for what is celebrated upon it.
strings.art.altar.li_flowers: **Flowers** — may adorn the altar in moderation according to the season; never during Lent, and only sparingly in Advent.
strings.art.altar.li_frontal: **The frontal** — an antependium may hang before the altar in the colour of the day.
strings.art.altar.p3: The linens used at the altar are white, blessed for sacred use, and handled with great care. Some cover the altar itself; others serve at the moment of Communion.
strings.art.altar.li_altarcloth: **The altar cloth (“fair linen”)** — the white cloth, traditionally of linen, that covers the altar table; in earlier custom three cloths were used together.
strings.art.altar.li_corporal: **The corporal** — a square white cloth unfolded at the centre of the altar, on which the chalice and paten rest so that no fragment of the Host is lost.
strings.art.altar.li_purificator: **The purificator** — a small folded cloth used to wipe the chalice and the priest's fingers.
strings.art.altar.li_pall: **The pall** — a stiff linen-covered square laid over the chalice to keep anything from falling into it.
strings.art.altar.p4: When a new altar is dedicated, the bishop anoints it with sacred chrism and incenses it. Five crosses are carved or marked into it — one at each corner and one in the centre — recalling the five wounds of Christ. In many altars the relics of a saint, often a martyr, are sealed within or beneath the altar stone, an ancient link to the tombs on which the early Church offered Mass.
strings.art.altar.callout.title: Why the kiss
strings.art.altar.callout.body: The priest kisses the altar because it stands for Christ, the cornerstone. At a solemn Mass it is also honoured with incense — the same reverence shown to the Gospel and to the gifts.
strings.sec.tabernacle.title: The Tabernacle
strings.sec.tabernacle.summary: The secure dwelling where the consecrated Eucharist is reserved, marked by the sanctuary lamp.
strings.art.tabernacle.title: The Tabernacle
strings.art.tabernacle.lead: The secure and honoured place where the Blessed Sacrament is reserved.
strings.art.tabernacle.image.caption: A traditional gilded tabernacle with Eucharistic wheat and vine ornament.
strings.art.tabernacle.p1: The tabernacle is the strong, locked repository in which the Church reserves the consecrated Eucharist after Mass. Its name recalls the tent or dwelling of God's presence in Scripture. Here the sign becomes more than symbolic: Christ himself remains sacramentally present under the appearances of bread.
strings.art.tabernacle.li_viaticum: **Viaticum for the dying** — the Church keeps the Eucharist ready as the final sacramental food for those nearing death.
strings.art.tabernacle.li_communion: **Communion outside Mass** — reserved hosts allow Holy Communion to be brought to the sick and to others unable to attend Mass.
strings.art.tabernacle.li_adoration: **Prayer and adoration** — the abiding presence of Christ invites the faithful to remain with him in silent prayer.
strings.art.tabernacle.p_lamp: A special lamp burns continually near the tabernacle whenever the Blessed Sacrament is reserved. Often red, it quietly announces that Christ is present and calls everyone who enters the church to reverence.
strings.art.tabernacle.p_place: A church ordinarily has one tabernacle. It must be immovable, made of solid and opaque material, securely locked, and placed in a distinguished location suited to prayer. Depending on the church, it may stand in the sanctuary or in a separate chapel of reservation.
strings.art.tabernacle.reverence.title: Reverence before the tabernacle
strings.art.tabernacle.reverence.body: Because the Eucharist is Christ truly present, Catholics genuflect toward the tabernacle when entering or leaving its presence. This act is directed to the Lord reserved within, not to the metal cabinet itself.
strings.art.tabernacle.distinction.title: Tabernacle and altar
strings.art.tabernacle.distinction.body: The altar is where the Eucharistic sacrifice is celebrated; the tabernacle is where the consecrated Eucharist is reserved afterward. They are closely related, but they serve distinct liturgical purposes.
strings.sec.mass.types.title: Types of Mass
strings.sec.mass.types.summary: One sacrifice, many occasions — from a weekday morning to the Easter Vigil.
strings.art.masstypes.title: Types of Mass
strings.art.masstypes.intro: The Mass may vary in occasion, form, or solemnity, but the Eucharist is always the same: the Body, Blood, Soul and Divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ. Good Friday alone is the exception — the one day of the year on which the Church offers no Mass at all.
strings.art.masstypes.sunday.title: Sunday Mass
strings.art.masstypes.sunday.body: The principal celebration of the Eucharist, which fulfils the Lord's Day obligation. It is the source and summit of the Christian life.
strings.art.masstypes.weekday.title: Weekday Mass
strings.art.masstypes.weekday.body: Celebrated on days other than Sunday, keeping our union with Christ and his Church through the whole week.
strings.art.masstypes.solemn.title: Solemn Mass
strings.art.masstypes.solemn.body: The most solemn form, usually with a deacon, incense and the fuller ceremonial. Used on major feasts and special occasions.
strings.art.masstypes.sung.title: Sung Mass
strings.art.masstypes.sung.body: The parts of the Mass — Kyrie, Gloria, Sanctus, Agnus Dei and the rest — are sung, reflecting the beauty and solemnity of worship.
strings.art.masstypes.low.title: Low Mass
strings.art.masstypes.low.body: Celebrated without singing and with fewer ministers — a simpler form, yet no less valid and no less reverent.
strings.art.masstypes.pontifical.title: Pontifical Mass
strings.art.masstypes.pontifical.body: Celebrated by a bishop or other prelate, expressing the Church's unity with her bishop. Usually very solemn.
strings.art.masstypes.nuptial.title: Nuptial Mass
strings.art.masstypes.nuptial.body: Celebrated in connection with the Sacrament of Matrimony, where the couple offer their union within the Eucharist.
strings.art.masstypes.funeral.title: Funeral or Requiem Mass
strings.art.masstypes.funeral.body: Offered for the deceased, commending the soul to God's mercy and giving hope in the resurrection.
strings.art.masstypes.votive.title: Votive Mass
strings.art.masstypes.votive.body: Offered for a particular devotion, intention, need or thanksgiving — for vocations, for peace, in thanksgiving, for the poor, and so on.
strings.art.masstypes.dead.title: Mass for the Dead
strings.art.masstypes.dead.body: Offered for the faithful departed, a spiritual help for the souls in purgatory.
strings.art.masstypes.chrism.title: Chrism Mass
strings.art.masstypes.chrism.body: Celebrated by the bishop, usually on the morning of Holy Thursday: the blessing of the holy oils and the renewal of priestly promises.
strings.art.masstypes.supper.title: Mass of the Lord's Supper
strings.art.masstypes.supper.body: On Holy Thursday, commemorating the Last Supper and the institution of the Eucharist and the priesthood. Often followed by the transfer of the Blessed Sacrament to the Altar of Repose.
strings.art.masstypes.vigil.title: Mass of the Easter Vigil
strings.art.masstypes.vigil.body: The “Mother of all Vigils”, which begins the celebration of Easter on Holy Saturday night. It includes the Liturgy of Light, the Liturgy of the Word, Baptism and the Eucharist.
strings.art.masstypes.same.title: The same sacrifice
strings.art.masstypes.same.body: All Masses are the same Eucharistic Sacrifice of Christ. They differ only in occasion, form, or degree of solemnity.
strings.art.masstypes.christmas.title: The Christmas Masses
strings.art.masstypes.christmas.body: Christmas has four Masses of its own — the Vigil Mass, the Mass during the Night, the Mass at Dawn, and the Mass during the Day. Each has its own readings and prayers, and together they unfold the mystery of the Word made flesh.
strings.art.masstypes.ashwed.title: Ash Wednesday Mass
strings.art.masstypes.ashwed.body: Opens Lent with the blessing and distribution of ashes, marking the forehead as a sign of repentance. A day of fasting and abstinence, though not a holy day of obligation.
strings.art.masstypes.palm.title: Palm Sunday Mass
strings.art.masstypes.palm.body: Palm Sunday of the Passion of the Lord opens Holy Week. It begins with the blessing of palms and a procession recalling Christ's entry into Jerusalem, and the Passion is proclaimed at the Mass.
strings.art.masstypes.goodfriday.title: Good Friday — no Mass is offered
strings.art.masstypes.goodfriday.body: Good Friday is the one day in the year when no Mass is celebrated anywhere in the Church. In its place the Church keeps the Celebration of the Lord's Passion: the Liturgy of the Word with the Passion according to St John, the solemn intercessions, the Adoration of the Cross, and Holy Communion from hosts consecrated the evening before.
strings.sec.mass.year.title: The Liturgical Year
strings.sec.mass.year.summary: Advent to Christ the King — the seasons the Church keeps, and their colours.
strings.art.year.title: The Liturgical Year
strings.art.year.lead: The seasons the Church keeps, and their colours.
strings.art.year.intro: The Church measures time by the mystery of Christ. Her year begins not in January but on the First Sunday of Advent, and it carries the faithful through his coming, his birth, his ministry, his passion, his resurrection, and the long green weeks of growth in between.
strings.art.year.advent.title: Advent
strings.art.year.advent.body: Preparing for the coming of Christ. Four weeks of watchful preparation for both his birth at Bethlehem and his return in glory, kept in hope rather than in mourning.
strings.art.year.christmas.title: Christmas
strings.art.year.christmas.body: Celebrating the birth and manifestation of Jesus. From Christmas Day through the Epiphany to the Baptism of the Lord, the Church celebrates the Word made flesh and his showing forth to the world.
strings.art.year.ordinary.title: Ordinary Time
strings.art.year.ordinary.body: Growing in faith through the life and teachings of Jesus. The longest season, and the one most easily misread: “ordinary” here means ordered and counted, not plain.
strings.art.year.lent.title: Lent
strings.art.year.lent.body: Repentance, prayer, fasting, and preparation for Easter. Forty days from Ash Wednesday given to prayer, fasting and almsgiving, preparing the faithful — and the catechumens — for the Easter sacraments.
strings.art.year.triduum.title: The Sacred Paschal Triduum
strings.art.year.triduum.body: The Passion, Death and Resurrection of Jesus. Three days from the evening of Holy Thursday to the evening of Easter Sunday — not three celebrations but one, and the summit of the whole year.
strings.art.year.easter.title: Easter
strings.art.year.easter.body: Celebrating Christ's Resurrection and his victory over sin and death. Fifty days of rejoicing from Easter Sunday to Pentecost — the Church's greatest season, longer than Lent that prepared for it.
strings.art.year.order.title: The order of the year
strings.art.year.order.8: Advent again — the year begins anew
strings.art.year.note.title: Two things worth remembering
strings.art.year.note.body: Ordinary Time is kept in two separate periods — between Christmas and Lent, and again from Pentecost until Advent. And the Sacred Paschal Triduum is the central celebration of the Christian year: everything else in the calendar leans towards it or flows from it.
strings.sec.mass.readings.title: The Cycle of Readings
strings.sec.mass.readings.summary: Years A, B and C — why the Sunday Gospel changes from year to year.
strings.art.cycles.title: Years A, B and C
strings.art.cycles.lead: Why the Sunday readings follow a three-year cycle.
strings.art.cycles.intro: At Sunday Mass the Church reads Scripture on a three-year cycle — Year A, Year B and Year C — so that over three years the faithful hear far more of the Bible than a single year could hold. Each year is built around one of the first three Gospels: Matthew, Mark or Luke. The plan comes from the reform of the Lectionary that followed the Second Vatican Council; before it, the Roman Missal repeated the same readings every year.
strings.art.cycles.now.label: This liturgical year
strings.art.cycles.now.body: Sundays follow Year {sunday}, and weekdays in Ordinary Time follow Year {weekday}. The cycle moves on at the First Sunday of Advent.
strings.art.cycles.a.title: Year A — Matthew
strings.art.cycles.a.body: Jesus as the fulfilment of the Scriptures and the teacher of the Kingdom. Matthew writes with the Law and the Prophets always in view, showing Jesus as the one they foretold, and gathers his teaching into five great discourses, beginning with the Sermon on the Mount.
strings.art.cycles.b.title: Year B — Mark
strings.art.cycles.b.body: Jesus' ministry, his suffering, and the call to follow him on the way of the cross. Mark is the shortest Gospel, so in the summer five Sundays (the 17th to the 21st in Ordinary Time) turn to John 6, the discourse on the Bread of Life.
strings.art.cycles.c.title: Year C — Luke
strings.art.cycles.c.body: Jesus' mercy, the salvation he brings, and his care for the poor and for sinners. Luke alone records the parables of the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son, and both are read in this year.
strings.art.cycles.john.title: The Gospel of John — every year
strings.art.cycles.john.body: John has no year of its own, because it is read in all three. It is heard on Christmas Day and through much of Lent — the Samaritan woman, the man born blind and the raising of Lazarus, which may be read in any year where catechumens are preparing for baptism. It returns in Holy Week, with the Passion according to John on every Good Friday, and on most Sundays of Easter.
strings.art.cycles.sunday.title: What is read on a Sunday
strings.art.cycles.sunday.1: First reading — usually from the Old Testament, chosen to echo that day's Gospel; in Eastertide, from the Acts of the Apostles.
strings.art.cycles.sunday.2: Responsorial Psalm — the assembly's sung or spoken response to the first reading.
strings.art.cycles.sunday.3: Second reading — from the letters of the Apostles or the Book of Revelation.
strings.art.cycles.sunday.4: Gospel — the high point of the Liturgy of the Word, for which everyone stands.
strings.art.cycles.why.title: Why three years
strings.art.cycles.why.1: So that the faithful hear more of the Bible.
strings.art.cycles.why.2: So that they meet Christ through the distinct voice of each Gospel.
strings.art.cycles.why.3: So that the whole of salvation history is set out more completely.
strings.art.cycles.why.4: So that the readings follow the liturgical year, from Advent and Christmas through Lent and Easter to Ordinary Time.
strings.art.cycles.weekday.title: Weekdays: Year I and Year II
strings.art.cycles.weekday.body: Weekday Masses have two readings, not three. In Ordinary Time the first reading follows a two-year cycle — Year I in odd-numbered years, Year II in even-numbered ones — while the weekday Gospels are the same every year. In Advent, Christmas, Lent and Easter, the weekday readings repeat annually.
strings.art.cycles.which.title: How to tell which year it is
strings.art.cycles.which.body: A liturgical year begins on the First Sunday of Advent and takes its number from the calendar year in which it ends. Divide that year by three: a remainder of 1 is Year A, a remainder of 2 is Year B, and a year that divides exactly is Year C. So the year ending in 2027 is Year B, and the one ending in 2028 is Year C.
strings.art.cycles.ordo.title: A word about “the Ordo”
strings.art.cycles.ordo.body: The three-year plan belongs to the Lectionary, and is set out in the Ordo Lectionum Missae — the Order of Readings for Mass, first published in 1969 and revised in 1981. In everyday parish use, “the Ordo” usually means something else: the annual liturgical calendar that tells priests what is celebrated each day, and with which readings and prayers.
strings.art.cycles.quote: “The treasures of the bible are to be opened up more lavishly, so that richer fare may be provided for the faithful at the table of God's word. In this way a more representative portion of the holy scriptures will be read to the people in the course of a prescribed number of years.”
strings.sec.mass.books.title: Books Used at Mass
strings.sec.mass.books.summary: The Lectionary, the Book of the Gospels and the Roman Missal.
strings.art.books.title: Books Used at Mass
strings.art.books.lead: The Lectionary, the Book of the Gospels and the Roman Missal.
strings.art.books.intro: Three books are used at almost every Mass, and each has its own place. Two of them hold the Word of God and belong at the ambo, where the readings are proclaimed. The third holds the prayers of the Mass and belongs at the altar and the chair, with the priest. Together they carry everything that is said aloud at Mass except the hymns.
strings.art.books.lectionary.title: The Lectionary
strings.art.books.lectionary.body: The book of the Scripture readings proclaimed at Mass: the first reading, the responsorial psalm, the second reading and the Gospel, each set out for its own day. The readings are not chosen by the priest but appointed by the Church, and the Lectionary is usually bound in several volumes — Sundays, weekdays, and Masses for particular occasions.
strings.art.books.lectionary.caption: Kept at the ambo, where the Word is proclaimed
strings.art.books.gospels.title: The Book of the Gospels
strings.art.books.gospels.body: Also called the Evangeliary, this book holds the Gospel passages alone, and it is the most richly bound of the three. A deacon or reader carries it aloft in the entrance procession and lays it on the altar; at the Gospel it is carried to the ambo, often with incense and candles, and kissed at the end of the reading. The honour is given not to the book but to Christ, who speaks in his own words.
strings.art.books.gospels.caption: Carried in procession, laid on the altar, kissed after the Gospel
strings.art.books.missal.title: The Roman Missal
strings.art.books.missal.body: The priest's book at the altar. It holds the prayers and texts of the Mass: the Order of Mass, the collect, the prayer over the offerings, the prefaces, the Eucharistic Prayers and the prayer after Communion, together with the prayers proper to each day of the year. It does not contain the readings, which is why the Lectionary is a separate book.
strings.art.books.missal.caption: Carried to the altar and the chair, for the prayers of the Mass
strings.art.books.reverence.title: How the Gospel book is honoured
strings.art.books.reverence.1: It is carried in the entrance procession, raised slightly, and never held closed against the body like an ordinary book.
strings.art.books.reverence.2: It rests on the altar until the Gospel, the only book given that place.
strings.art.books.reverence.3: The deacon or priest asks a blessing before carrying it to the ambo.
strings.art.books.reverence.4: It may be honoured with incense and flanked by candles, and everyone stands.
strings.art.books.reverence.5: At the end the reader kisses it, saying quietly: “Through the words of the Gospel may our sins be wiped away.”
strings.art.books.optional.title: Two books, one Gospel
strings.art.books.optional.body: The Book of the Gospels is not required. Where a parish does not have one, the Gospel is simply proclaimed from the Lectionary, which contains it too. The Book of the Gospels exists to give those words a book of their own, and a procession worthy of them.
strings.art.books.others.title: Other books you may see
strings.art.books.others.body: A choir or cantor may use the Roman Gradual or a hymnal for the chants; the ritual books are brought out when a baptism, a wedding or an ordination takes place within Mass; and at a bishop's Mass the ceremonial of bishops is followed. In English, the Missal was for years called the Sacramentary — the name changed with the current translation, which came into use in 2011.
strings.art.books.quote: “Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light for my path.”
strings.sec.church.title: Inside a Catholic Church
strings.sec.church.summary: A map of the church building, and the furnishings of the sanctuary.
strings.art.churchmap.title: The Church Like a Map
strings.art.churchmap.lead: Fifteen places you have seen — and what each one is for.
strings.art.churchmap.image.caption: A Catholic church, numbered from the door to the sacristy.
strings.art.churchmap.p1: A Catholic church is more than a hall for a crowd. It is the house where the Church gathers to pray, to hear the Word, to celebrate the sacraments and to be sent out again. Its layout leads the eye and the steps of the faithful from the entrance toward the altar, and every place has its purpose.
strings.art.churchmap.li_narthex: **1. Narthex** — the entrance and welcoming area, between the outside world and the church proper.
strings.art.churchmap.li_nave: **2. Nave** — the main area where the faithful gather.
strings.art.churchmap.li_font: **4. Baptismal font** — where Baptism is celebrated, often near the entrance because Baptism is the doorway to the Christian life.
strings.art.churchmap.li_confessional: **5. Confessional** — where the sacrament of Reconciliation is celebrated.
strings.art.churchmap.li_stations: **6. Stations of the Cross** — devotional images along the walls that recall Christ's Passion.
strings.art.churchmap.li_sanctuary: **8. Sanctuary** — the sacred area around the altar.
strings.art.churchmap.li_altar: **9. Altar** — the table of the Eucharistic sacrifice.
strings.art.churchmap.li_tabernacle: **10. Tabernacle** — where the Blessed Sacrament is reserved.
strings.art.churchmap.li_lamp: **11. Sanctuary lamp** — shows the real presence of Jesus.
strings.art.churchmap.li_crucifix: **12. Crucifix** — reminds us of Christ's sacrifice.
strings.art.churchmap.li_chair: **13. Presider's chair** — the chair of the priest who presides.
strings.art.churchmap.li_credence: **14. Credence table** — holds the items needed for Mass.
strings.art.churchmap.li_sacristy: **15. Sacristy** — where vestments and sacred vessels are prepared.
strings.art.churchmap.callout.title: One church, one direction
strings.art.churchmap.callout.body: From the font at the door to the altar and tabernacle at the far end, the building tells a story: baptised into Christ, we are fed at his table and sent back into the world. The sanctuary is where all the lines of the church converge.
strings.art.sanctuary.title: The Sanctuary and Its Furnishings
strings.art.sanctuary.lead: The altar, the ambo, the tabernacle and the other furnishings around them.
strings.art.sanctuary.image.caption: The principal furnishings of a traditional sanctuary.
strings.art.sanctuary.p1: The sanctuary is the raised, set-apart part of the church where the sacred rites are carried out. Each piece of furniture in it serves a particular action of the liturgy: proclaiming the Word, offering the sacrifice, reserving the Eucharist, or preparing the vessels.
strings.art.sanctuary.li_altar: **1. Altar table** — the principal sacred table where the Eucharistic sacrifice is celebrated.
strings.art.sanctuary.li_ambo: **2. Ambo** — the place set aside for proclaiming the readings and the Gospel.
strings.art.sanctuary.li_tabernacle: **3. Tabernacle** — the secure sacred place where the Blessed Sacrament is reserved.
strings.art.sanctuary.li_lamp: **4. Sanctuary lamp** — a lamp placed near the tabernacle to signify the presence of the Blessed Sacrament.
strings.art.sanctuary.li_retablo: **5. Retablo (reredos)** — the decorative structure behind the altar, often holding statues, paintings or other sacred imagery.
strings.art.sanctuary.li_credence: **6. Credence table** — a table in or near the sanctuary for preparing and holding the liturgical vessels and books.
strings.art.sanctuary.li_relic: **7. Relic** — a relic of a saint, traditionally placed beneath or within an altar.
strings.art.sanctuary.li_rail: **8. Altar rail (communion rail)** — a railing that traditionally separates the sanctuary from the rest of the church and was historically used by the faithful when receiving Holy Communion.
strings.art.sanctuary.relic.title: Why a relic in the altar
strings.art.sanctuary.relic.body: The Church has long placed the relics of martyrs and other saints beneath the altar, recalling the early Christians who celebrated the Eucharist over the tombs of the martyrs. The custom is retained, though the Roman rite does not require it for every altar.
strings.art.sanctuary.rail.title: Altar rails today
strings.art.sanctuary.rail.body: Many churches removed their altar rails after the Second Vatican Council, and Communion is now commonly received standing in a procession. Some churches keep or restore the rail, and the faithful may receive kneeling there. Both practices are legitimate.
strings.sec.mass.bells.title: The Bells of the Church
strings.sec.mass.bells.summary: From the small bell rung at the altar to the great bell that sounds from the tower.
strings.art.bells.title: The Bells of the Church
strings.art.bells.lead: Bronze voices that mark the sacred moments of worship, prayer and procession.
strings.art.bells.intro: Bells have called the faithful to prayer and marked the sacred action of the Mass since the earliest centuries of the Church. Their size and use vary — from a small handbell at the altar to the great bell that sounds from the tower — but each shares the same purpose: to turn hearts toward God at a holy moment.
strings.art.bells.sanctus.title: The Sanctus Bell
strings.art.bells.sanctus.body: A small bell with a handle, rung by a server at significant moments of the Mass — above all at the consecration — to draw the attention of the faithful to what is happening on the altar.
strings.art.bells.sanctus.caption: Used during Mass, traditionally at the consecration
strings.art.bells.chime.title: The Four-Bell Altar Chime
strings.art.bells.chime.body: Four small bells arranged on a central handle in the shape of a cross, rung together during the Eucharistic celebration, especially at the consecration, in churches that favour this fuller chime.
strings.art.bells.chime.caption: Rung during the Eucharistic celebration, especially at the consecration
strings.art.bells.tower.title: The Church Tower Bell
strings.art.bells.tower.body: A large bell mounted in a church tower or bell tower, rung to call the faithful to prayer and Mass, and which may also announce the Angelus or other occasions.
strings.art.bells.tower.caption: Calls the faithful to prayer and Mass
strings.art.bells.carillon.title: Carillon Bells
strings.art.bells.carillon.body: A set of tuned bells of different sizes, played together from a keyboard. Carillons produce musical chimes and are usually found in larger churches and basilicas.
strings.art.bells.carillon.caption: A set of tuned bells, played together from a keyboard
strings.art.bells.altar.title: The Altar Bell
strings.art.bells.altar.body: A small bell, or a small set of bells, placed beside or attached near the altar and used during the liturgy according to local practice.
strings.art.bells.altar.caption: Placed beside the altar, used according to local practice
strings.art.bells.note.title: Local custom
strings.art.bells.note.body: The exact use of bells can vary according to the liturgical norms of the Roman Rite and local custom — not every parish uses every kind described here.
strings.sec.mass.oils.title: The Three Holy Oils
strings.sec.mass.oils.summary: Oil of the Catechumens, Sacred Chrism and Oil of the Sick — blessed by the bishop for use across the year.
strings.art.oils.title: The Three Holy Oils
strings.art.oils.lead: Blessed or consecrated by the bishop, and used throughout the sacramental life of the Church.
strings.art.oils.intro: The Catholic Church uses three principal holy oils, normally blessed or consecrated by the bishop at the Chrism Mass during Holy Week. Made from olive oil, they are sacramentals through which the Church asks God's blessing, and each has its own name, abbreviation and use.
strings.art.oils.oc.title: Oil of the Catechumens (Oleum Catechumenorum)
strings.art.oils.oc.body: Used for anointing catechumens preparing for Baptism. It symbolises the strength and protection they need as they prepare to enter the Christian life, and is usually abbreviated OC.
strings.art.oils.oc.caption: Blessed by the bishop; used before Baptism
strings.art.oils.sc.title: Sacred Chrism (Sacrum Chrisma)
strings.art.oils.sc.body: A mixture of olive oil and fragrant balsam, consecrated by the bishop rather than simply blessed. It is used in Baptism, Confirmation and Holy Orders, and in the dedication of churches and altars, and symbolises being anointed and strengthened by the Holy Spirit. Usually abbreviated SC or Chr.
strings.art.oils.sc.caption: Consecrated by the bishop; used in Baptism, Confirmation and Holy Orders
strings.art.oils.oi.title: Oil of the Sick (Oleum Infirmorum)
strings.art.oils.oi.body: Used in the Sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick. It is associated with healing, comfort and strengthening for those who are sick, and is usually abbreviated OI.
strings.art.oils.oi.caption: Blessed by the bishop; used in the Anointing of the Sick
strings.art.oils.note.title: Blessed at the Chrism Mass
strings.art.oils.note.body: All three oils are normally blessed or consecrated once a year by the bishop at the Chrism Mass, usually celebrated on the morning of Holy Thursday, and are then distributed to every parish of the diocese for use throughout the year.
strings.sec.mass.altar_sacristy.title: Altar and Sacristy
strings.sec.mass.altar_sacristy.summary: Two places in the church, easily confused — the table of sacrifice, and the room where it's all prepared.
strings.art.altarsac.title: Altar and Sacristy
strings.art.altarsac.lead: Two places at the heart of every Mass — one where it is offered, one where it is prepared.
strings.art.altarsac.intro: The altar and the sacristy are both essential to the Mass, and easy to confuse by name alone. One is the sacred table where the Eucharistic Sacrifice is offered; the other is the working room, usually nearby, where the clergy and servers vest and everything needed for Mass is made ready.
strings.art.altarsac.altar.caption: Altar — the sacred table of the Eucharistic Sacrifice
strings.art.altarsac.sacristy.caption: Sacristy — where the ministers and liturgical items are prepared
strings.art.altarsac.altar.what: The sacred table where the Eucharistic Sacrifice is offered during Mass — the central focus of the church's sanctuary.
strings.art.altarsac.sacristy.what: A room, usually located near the sanctuary, where the clergy and ministers prepare for liturgical celebrations.
strings.art.altarsac.sacristy.simple: Where the ministers and liturgical items are prepared for the celebration.
strings.art.altarsac.points.title: At the altar, and in the sacristy
strings.art.altarsac.altar.k1: The bread and wine are presented, and the Eucharistic Prayer is offered.
strings.art.altarsac.altar.k2: The bread and wine become the Body and Blood of Christ.
strings.art.altarsac.altar.k3: The altar is honoured with a kiss by the priest and deacon.
strings.art.altarsac.altar.k4: It symbolises Christ himself, as well as the table of the Lord.
strings.art.altarsac.sacristy.k1: Sacred vestments such as the chasuble, stole and dalmatic are stored there.
strings.art.altarsac.sacristy.k2: Liturgical books and other items used at Mass are kept there.
strings.art.altarsac.sacristy.k3: The sacred vessels are prepared there before and after Mass.
strings.art.altarsac.sacristy.k4: It provides a place for the priest, deacon and servers to vest.
strings.art.altarsac.keydiff.title: In simple terms
strings.art.altarsac.keydiff.body: The sacristy is more like the church's preparation and storage room for sacred things, while the altar is the place of Eucharistic worship itself.
strings.art.altarsac.ccc.title: The altar, in the Catechism
strings.art.altarsac.ccc.body: The Catechism teaches that the altar represents both the sacrificial altar and the table of the Lord (CCC 1383).
strings.sec.mass.cathedra_chair.title: Cathedra or Presider's Chair?
strings.sec.mass.cathedra_chair.summary: The bishop's chair, and the chair every priest sits in — two very different seats.
strings.art.cathedra.title: Cathedra or Presider's Chair?
strings.art.cathedra.lead: The bishop's chair, and the chair every priest sits in during Mass — easy to mix up, very different in meaning.
strings.art.cathedra.intro: Every church has a chair for the one who presides at Mass, but only a cathedral has a cathedra — the bishop's own chair, and the reason a cathedral is called a cathedral at all.
strings.art.cathedra.cathedra.caption: Cathedra — the bishop's chair
strings.art.cathedra.chair.caption: Presider's chair — the celebrant's chair
strings.art.cathedra.cathedra.meaning: The bishop's office of teaching and governing his diocese.
strings.art.cathedra.cathedra.usedduring: Solemn diocesan liturgies, ordinarily reserved to the bishop.
strings.art.cathedra.chair.meaning: His role as presider of the liturgical celebration.
strings.art.cathedra.chair.usedduring: The parts of Mass when the priest is seated.
strings.art.cathedra.chair.canuse: Yes — though it is not the bishop's cathedra.
strings.art.cathedra.points.title: Worth remembering
strings.art.cathedra.cathedra.k1: The word cathedra means “chair”; cathedral takes its name directly from it.
strings.art.cathedra.cathedra.k2: It symbolises the bishop's authority to teach and govern in his own name, not merely to preside.
strings.art.cathedra.cathedra.k3: A diocese has only one cathedra, and it stands in the cathedral church alone.
strings.art.cathedra.chair.k1: Found in the sanctuary of every church, not only cathedrals.
strings.art.cathedra.chair.k2: Remains distinct from a bishop's cathedra even when a bishop celebrates Mass there using his own chair.
strings.art.cathedra.chair.k3: Used for the parts of Mass when the priest sits: the readings before the Gospel, the homily, and some moments of the Liturgy of the Eucharist.
strings.art.cathedra.name.title: Gives the cathedral its name
strings.art.cathedra.name.body: A cathedral is, by definition, simply the church that houses the bishop's cathedra — the word comes directly from it.
strings.art.cathedra.remember.title: Easy to remember
strings.art.cathedra.remember.body: Cathedra = the bishop's chair. Presider's chair = the celebrant's chair. Every bishop's cathedra is a presider's chair, but not every presider's chair is a cathedra.
strings.sec.mass.altar_parts.title: Altar Table, Altar Frontal, and Retablo
strings.sec.mass.altar_parts.summary: Three parts of the sanctuary around the altar, easily confused by name alone.
strings.art.altarparts.title: Altar Table, Altar Frontal, and Retablo
strings.art.altarparts.lead: Three parts of the sanctuary, easily confused by name alone.
strings.art.altarparts.intro: The altar table, its frontal and the retablo behind it are often confused, but each has its own distinct purpose: one is the sacred table itself, one is a decorative covering on its front, and one is the artistic structure that rises behind or above it.
strings.art.altarparts.table.title: The Altar Table
strings.art.altarparts.table.body: The actual sacred table on which the Eucharistic Sacrifice is offered during Mass, and on which the bread and wine are placed (CCC 1182).
strings.art.altarparts.table.caption: The sacred table of the Eucharistic Sacrifice
strings.art.altarparts.frontal.title: The Altar Frontal
strings.art.altarparts.frontal.body: The decorative covering or facing on the front of the altar, often bearing a cross, sacred images or embroidery, usually in the colour of the liturgical season. It serves mainly a decorative and symbolic purpose.
strings.art.altarparts.frontal.caption: The decorative facing on the front of the altar
strings.art.altarparts.retablo.title: The Retablo
strings.art.altarparts.retablo.body: The artistic or architectural structure behind or above the altar, which may hold statues, paintings and other sacred artwork, drawing the eye toward Christ and the mysteries celebrated at the altar. Also called a reredos.
strings.art.altarparts.retablo.caption: The structure rising behind the altar
strings.art.altarparts.remember.title: Easy to remember
strings.art.altarparts.remember.body: Altar Table = the sacred table. Altar Frontal = the front decoration. Retablo = the structure behind the altar.
strings.sec.mass.basilica_cathedral.title: Basilicas and Cathedrals
strings.sec.mass.basilica_cathedral.summary: What makes a church a basilica or a cathedral, and the two ranks of basilica — major and minor.
strings.art.basicath.title: Basilica or Cathedral?
strings.art.basicath.lead: A title of honour from the Pope, and the seat of a bishop — easy to confuse, and sometimes the same church.
strings.art.basicath.intro: Both words name great churches, and both are often used loosely. But they answer different questions. A basilica is a church the Pope has honoured with a special title; a cathedral is the church where a bishop has his chair, the cathedra, and from which he shepherds his diocese.
strings.art.basicath.basilica.caption: Basilica — a church honoured with a special title
strings.art.basicath.cathedral.caption: Cathedral — the main church of a bishop's diocese
strings.art.basicath.basilica.what: A major church given special honour because of its history, its importance, or its place in the life and devotion of the Church.
strings.art.basicath.basilica.who: The Pope, who grants the title.
strings.art.basicath.basilica.mark: Its bond with the Pope, shown by the papal keys, the umbraculum (a striped canopy) and the tintinnabulum (a processional bell).
strings.art.basicath.basilica.howmany: As many as the Pope chooses to honour — four major basilicas in Rome, and well over a thousand minor basilicas worldwide.
strings.art.basicath.basilica.example: St Peter's Basilica, Vatican City — a basilica, but not a cathedral.
strings.art.basicath.cathedral.what: The main church of a diocese: the seat of the bishop and the centre of his teaching, worship and pastoral care.
strings.art.basicath.cathedral.who: The presence of the bishop's cathedra — a church is a cathedral because his chair is there.
strings.art.basicath.cathedral.mark: The cathedra, the bishop's chair, from which the word "cathedral" comes.
strings.art.basicath.cathedral.example: St John Lateran, Rome — the Pope's own cathedral as Bishop of Rome, and also a major basilica.
strings.art.basicath.points.title: Worth remembering
strings.art.basicath.basilica.k1: The four major (papal) basilicas are all in Rome: St John Lateran, St Peter's, St Mary Major and St Paul Outside the Walls.
strings.art.basicath.basilica.k2: Every other basilica is a minor basilica, a title the Holy See grants on request after reviewing the church's history and liturgical life.
strings.art.basicath.basilica.k3: A basilica is expected to be a model of liturgy and devotion for the local Church, and to celebrate papal feasts with particular care.
strings.art.basicath.basilica.k4: The word is older than the title: in ancient Rome a basilica was a great public hall, the shape many early churches borrowed.
strings.art.basicath.cathedral.k1: Size and style have nothing to do with it — a small, plain church is a cathedral if the bishop's chair is there.
strings.art.basicath.cathedral.k2: It is the mother church of the diocese, where the bishop ordains priests and blesses the holy oils at the Chrism Mass.
strings.art.basicath.cathedral.k3: The church of an archbishop who leads a province is often called a metropolitan cathedral.
strings.art.basicath.cathedral.k4: Many cathedrals are Gothic or Romanesque, but that is history and taste, not a requirement.
strings.art.basicath.both.title: Can a church be both?
strings.art.basicath.both.body: Yes. Many cathedrals have also been made basilicas, and the Pope's own cathedral, St John Lateran, is both a cathedral and a major basilica. But a church can be either one without the other: St Peter's is a basilica and not a cathedral, while many cathedrals have never received the basilica title.
strings.art.basicath.short.title: In short
strings.art.basicath.short.body: A basilica is a church with special status and privileges granted by the Pope. A cathedral is the main church of a bishop's diocese and the seat of his authority.
strings.art.basrank.title: Major and Minor Basilicas
strings.art.basrank.lead: Every basilica is honoured by the Pope, but not all at the same rank: four great churches of Rome, and many more around the world.
strings.art.basrank.intro: A basilica is a church bound to the Pope by a title of honour. The Church recognises two ranks of that title. The major basilicas are the four ancient papal churches of Rome; every other basilica in the world is a minor basilica, a title the Pope grants to churches of particular importance to the life of the Church.
strings.art.basrank.major.caption: Major Basilica — the four papal churches of Rome
strings.art.basrank.minor.caption: Minor Basilica — a title of honour granted worldwide
strings.art.basrank.major.rank: The highest-ranking churches in the Catholic Church.
strings.art.basrank.major.who: No grant is made: the rank is ancient, belonging to the Pope's own churches as Bishop of Rome.
strings.art.basrank.major.where: All in Rome — St Peter's in Vatican City, and three in the city itself that belong to the Holy See.
strings.art.basrank.major.mark: A papal altar, where only the Pope or a priest he delegates may celebrate, and a Holy Door opened in Jubilee years.
strings.art.basrank.major.example: St John Lateran, the cathedral of Rome and the first in rank of the four.
strings.art.basrank.minor.rank: An honorary title that places a church in a special bond with the Pope.
strings.art.basrank.minor.who: The Pope, through the Dicastery for Divine Worship, at the request of the local bishop.
strings.art.basrank.minor.howmany: Around 1,900, and more are named every year.
strings.art.basrank.minor.where: Throughout the world, on every inhabited continent.
strings.art.basrank.minor.mark: The umbraculum (a striped canopy), the tintinnabulum (a processional bell), and the crossed papal keys on its banners, furnishings and seal.
strings.art.basrank.minor.example: Our Lady of Good Health, Velankanni — a minor basilica since 1962.
strings.art.basrank.points.title: Worth remembering
strings.art.basrank.major.k1: The four are St John Lateran, St Peter's, St Mary Major and St Paul Outside the Walls. Until 2006 they were called patriarchal basilicas; today they are the papal basilicas.
strings.art.basrank.major.k2: Their four Holy Doors are opened together in a Holy Year, and pilgrims visit all four to gain the Jubilee indulgence.
strings.art.basrank.major.k3: St Peter's is the best known, but St John Lateran ranks first, because it is the Pope's cathedral — "mother and head of all churches".
strings.art.basrank.major.k4: Some lists count six by adding San Francesco and Santa Maria degli Angeli in Assisi. Those two are papal basilicas with papal altars, but by rank they are minor basilicas.
strings.art.basrank.minor.k1: The 1989 decree Domus Ecclesiae sets the conditions: a consecrated church of some size, with clergy to serve it and a living liturgical and pastoral life.
strings.art.basrank.minor.k2: History, relics, a revered image, sacred art or pilgrimage often lie behind the request, but the title honours what happens inside the church, not its fame alone.
strings.art.basrank.minor.k3: The faithful may gain a plenary indulgence there on set days, among them the titular feast, Sts Peter and Paul on 29 June, and the anniversary of the title, under the usual conditions.
strings.art.basrank.minor.k4: The earliest known grant of the title went to San Nicola da Tolentino in Italy, in 1783.
strings.art.basrank.style.title: A title of honour, not a style
strings.art.basrank.style.body: "Basilica" names a status, not a kind of building. The word comes from the great public halls of ancient Rome, whose long-naved plan the first churches borrowed, but today a modern concrete church can be a basilica while a vast Gothic cathedral may never have received the title.
strings.art.basrank.short.title: In short
strings.art.basrank.short.body: There are four major basilicas, all in Rome, and they outrank every other church. Every other basilica is a minor basilica: a church anywhere in the world that the Pope has honoured for its importance to the life of the Church.
strings.sec.mass.roles.title: Liturgical Roles
strings.sec.mass.roles.summary: Altar server, acolyte and sacristan — different ministries, one work: to serve God and his Church.
strings.art.roles.title: Altar Server, Acolyte and Sacristan
strings.art.roles.lead: Three roles that serve the Mass, often confused because their work looks alike.
strings.art.roles.intro: At every Mass, people besides the priest and deacon help the liturgy unfold. Some carry the cross and candles, some prepare the altar, some have set everything out long before the first bell. These are different ministries, with different foundations in the Church's law, but one work: to serve God and his Church.
strings.art.roles.roles.title: Three roles
strings.art.roles.server.title: Altar Server
strings.art.roles.server.caption: Assists the priest and deacon during Mass
strings.art.roles.server.body: Altar servers carry the processional cross and candles, hold the Missal, bring the cruets and the water for the washing of hands, ring the bells and carry the thurible. Serving is not an instituted ministry: a server is appointed by the parish, usually a lay person and often a young one. Since 1994 girls and women may serve as well as boys and men, where the bishop permits it. Many priests first heard their vocation while serving at the altar.
strings.art.roles.acolyte.title: Instituted Acolyte
strings.art.roles.acolyte.caption: An instituted ministry of service at the altar
strings.art.roles.acolyte.body: An acolyte is installed by the bishop in a stable ministry, one of the two lay ministries that Pope St Paul VI kept when he reformed the minor orders in 1972. The acolyte assists the priest and deacon, prepares the altar and the sacred vessels, purifies them after Communion, and may distribute Holy Communion as an extraordinary minister when needed. Seminarians receive this ministry on the way to ordination, and since Pope Francis's Spiritus Domini (2021) it is open to lay men and women alike.
strings.art.roles.sacristan.title: Sacristan
strings.art.roles.sacristan.caption: Prepares and cares for the church's liturgical things
strings.art.roles.sacristan.body: The sacristan looks after the sacristy and everything the liturgy needs: the Missal and Lectionary, the chalice and paten, the vessels for Communion, the bread and wine, the vestments in the colour of the day, candles, incense and the thurible, and holy water. The Church asks that the sacristan arrange the books, vestments and other things carefully. A sacristan need not be an altar server or an instituted acolyte, and often serves quietly before anyone else arrives.
strings.art.roles.glance.title: At a glance
strings.art.roles.glance.server.value: Assists the priest and deacon. At Mass: carries the cross and candles, helps at the altar, carries incense, holds the Missal.
strings.art.roles.glance.acolyte.value: An instituted ministry of service at the altar. At Mass: assists the priest and deacon, prepares the altar, and may give Holy Communion as an extraordinary minister.
strings.art.roles.glance.sacristan.value: Prepares and cares for the church's liturgical things. Before Mass: sets out the vestments, vessels, books, bread and wine, and candles.
strings.art.roles.same.title: The same tasks, not the same ministry
strings.art.roles.same.body: An instituted acolyte and an ordinary altar server can be seen doing some of the same things at Mass, such as carrying candles or bringing the vessels to the altar. But they are not the same ministry: the acolyte has been installed by the bishop in a stable office of the Church, while the server helps by appointment of the parish. Only the instituted acolyte is, by law, an extraordinary minister of Holy Communion.
strings.art.roles.quote: “Whoever serves me must follow me, and where I am, there also will my servant be.”
strings.sec.mass.towers.title: Church Towers
strings.sec.mass.towers.summary: Bell towers, spires, flèches and domes — fifteen kinds of tower, and what each one is for.
strings.art.towers.title: Types of Church Towers
strings.art.towers.lead: Different designs, one purpose: to call people to prayer and give glory to God.
strings.art.towers.intro: A church tower is the first thing most people see of a church, often from miles away. Towers began as a practical answer to a practical need, a high place to hang the bells that called the faithful to Mass, and grew into one of the great signs of Christian architecture: a finger of stone pointing to heaven. Here are the kinds you are most likely to meet, and how to tell them apart.
strings.art.towers.bell.name: Bell Tower (Campanile)
strings.art.towers.bell.desc: A tower built to house the church bells, which ring for Mass, for the Angelus and at weddings and funerals. It may rise from the church itself or stand beside it. Campanile is the Italian word, and Italy has some of the most famous, such as St Mark's Campanile in Venice.
strings.art.towers.steeple.name: Steeple
strings.art.towers.steeple.desc: The whole of a tall tower together with the spire on top of it, rising above the church roof. Steeple is the everyday word for a church's tower and spire seen as one, and it is the outline most people picture when they think of a village church.
strings.art.towers.spire.name: Spire
strings.art.towers.spire.desc: The tapering, pointed top that crowns a tower, often very tall and slender. A spire is part of a steeple, not a tower in its own right. Salisbury Cathedral's spire, at 123 metres, is the tallest in Britain.
strings.art.towers.clock.name: Clock Tower
strings.art.towers.clock.desc: A church tower with a large clock face, or one on each side. Before watches were common, the church clock kept time for the whole town, and its bells struck the hours for people working in the fields.
strings.art.towers.fleche.name: Flèche
strings.art.towers.fleche.desc: A small, slender spire rising from the ridge of the roof, usually above the crossing, rather than from a full tower. The flèche of Notre-Dame de Paris fell in the fire of 2019 and was rebuilt to its old design before the cathedral reopened in December 2024.
strings.art.towers.crossing.name: Crossing Tower
strings.art.towers.crossing.desc: A tower built over the crossing, where the nave meets the transepts in a cross-shaped church. It lets light pour down into the heart of the church, often through a lantern of windows, right above the place where the altar traditionally stands.
strings.art.towers.west.name: West Tower
strings.art.towers.west.desc: A single tower at the western end of the church, the end opposite the altar and usually where the main door is, since churches have traditionally faced east towards the rising sun. It is the common shape of countless English and German parish churches.
strings.art.towers.twin.name: Twin Towers
strings.art.towers.twin.desc: Two matching towers flanking the main façade, framing the great west door like a gateway. Cologne Cathedral and Notre-Dame de Paris are famous examples. The pair gives the front of a great church its solemn, welcoming symmetry.
strings.art.towers.central.name: Central Tower
strings.art.towers.central.desc: A tower placed at the centre of the church building. In a cross-shaped church the central tower and the crossing tower are usually one and the same; the name simply describes where it stands rather than what it stands over.
strings.art.towers.detached.name: Detached Bell Tower
strings.art.towers.detached.desc: A bell tower standing apart from the church, a custom especially common in Italy. The best known in the world is the Leaning Tower of Pisa, which is in fact the campanile of Pisa Cathedral; Giotto's Campanile beside Florence Cathedral is another.
strings.art.towers.gable.name: Bell Gable (Campanile a Vela)
strings.art.towers.gable.desc: Not a tower at all, but a wall rising above the roof with arched openings for the bells, often on the façade. Called campanile a vela in Italian and espadaña in Spanish, it is common on small chapels and on the old missions of Spain and the Americas.
strings.art.towers.onion.name: Onion-Domed Tower
strings.art.towers.onion.desc: A tower topped by a bulbous, onion-shaped dome. It is the classic crown of Russian and other Eastern Christian churches, and also of many Catholic churches in Bavaria, Austria and Central Europe, where baroque builders made it their own.
strings.art.towers.romanesque.name: Romanesque Tower
strings.art.towers.romanesque.desc: A massive, square tower of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, with thick walls, round arches and small paired windows. Romanesque towers look like fortresses of faith, built to last and to stand firm.
strings.art.towers.gothic.name: Gothic Tower
strings.art.towers.gothic.desc: A tall tower full of pointed arches, pinnacles and tracery, all lines rushing upwards, often crowned by an openwork spire. Gothic builders of the twelfth to sixteenth centuries made height itself a prayer, as in the soaring towers of Cologne Cathedral.
strings.art.towers.baroque.name: Baroque Tower
strings.art.towers.baroque.desc: A richly decorated tower of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, stepped in stages and finished with curved cupolas, lanterns and sculpture. Baroque towers celebrate the joy and splendour of the faith, especially in Italy, Spain, Austria and Latin America.
strings.art.towers.purpose.title: Different designs, one purpose
strings.art.towers.purpose.body: Whatever its shape, a church tower serves the same ends: it carries the bells that call people to prayer, marks the church from afar as a house of God, and lifts the eye from the street to the sky. Many towers are crowned with a cross or a weathercock, the cock recalling St Peter and the call to stay awake in faith.
strings.art.towers.quote: “Walk about Zion, go all around it, count its towers.”
strings.art.chalices.title: Types of Chalices
strings.art.chalices.lead: Many shapes and styles, one purpose: to hold the Precious Blood at the Eucharist.
strings.art.chalices.intro: The chalice is the cup in which wine is offered and consecrated at Mass, becoming the Precious Blood of Christ. Chalices differ in how they are used, how they are made and the age whose art they reflect, but the basic function never changes. Here are the kinds and styles you are most likely to see.
strings.art.chalices.mass.name: Mass Chalice
strings.art.chalices.mass.desc: The principal chalice used by the priest or bishop celebrating Mass, the one placed on the corporal at the altar and lifted at the consecration. It is usually the finest chalice a parish owns, and many priests receive their own at ordination.
strings.art.chalices.communion.name: Communion Chalice
strings.art.chalices.communion.desc: A chalice used when the faithful receive Holy Communion under both kinds, the Precious Blood as well as the Host. Several may be needed at a large Mass, each held by a priest, deacon or extraordinary minister of Holy Communion.
strings.art.chalices.concelebration.name: Concelebration Chalice
strings.art.chalices.concelebration.desc: When several priests concelebrate, additional chalices may be prepared and consecrated alongside the principal one, so that each concelebrant can receive the Precious Blood. These are often a matched set made to sit together on the altar.
strings.art.chalices.travel.name: Travel or Portable Chalice
strings.art.chalices.travel.desc: A smaller, practical chalice for priests who celebrate Mass away from a church: on pilgrimage, in hospitals, at sea or in mission lands. Many unscrew into parts and fit in a fitted case with a small paten, a style familiar from military chaplains' Mass kits.
strings.art.chalices.baroque.name: Baroque Chalice
strings.art.chalices.baroque.desc: A richly decorated style of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, with embossed cherubs, flowers and scrollwork, a swelling, ornate stem and a broad, heavily worked base. Many are still in use in old parishes across Europe and Latin America.
strings.art.chalices.gothic.name: Gothic Chalice
strings.art.chalices.gothic.desc: A style inspired by medieval Gothic art, often with a six-lobed foot, a jewelled or enamelled knop in the stem, and architectural details like tiny pinnacles and window tracery. Gothic chalices were widely revived in the nineteenth century.
strings.art.chalices.romanesque.name: Romanesque Chalice
strings.art.chalices.romanesque.desc: An older style linked to Romanesque church art of the eleventh and twelfth centuries: a wide, shallow bowl, a short stem with a round knop and a broad, round foot, giving a heavy, solid appearance.
strings.art.chalices.modern.name: Modern Chalice
strings.art.chalices.modern.desc: A simpler design widely used since the twentieth century, with clean lines and little ornament, letting the form and the noble metal speak for themselves while still following every requirement the Church sets for sacred vessels.
strings.art.chalices.norms.title: What every chalice must be
strings.art.chalices.norms.body: Whatever its style, a chalice must be made of a noble material that does not absorb liquid, usually gold or silver, or another metal gilded on the inside. Glass, earthenware, clay and other breakable materials are not permitted. A chalice is blessed before it is first used, and it is reserved for the Eucharist alone.
strings.art.chalices.styles.title: Styles, not different sacraments
strings.art.chalices.styles.body: These are names for uses and artistic styles, not different kinds of sacred vessel or different rites. The Mass is the same whether the chalice is a Gothic treasure or a plain modern cup: in each, the wine becomes the Blood of Christ.
strings.art.chalices.quote: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”
